full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ: This appeal by special leave is directed against a decision of the High Court Division dated 14 July 1993 in first Appeal No. 87 of 1986 confirming the Subordinate Judge's Judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 46 of 1979. Questions raised in this appeal are whether specific performance of contract for sale of the land in suit should have been refused in the facts and circumstances of the case on the grounds that the plaintiff-respondent violated an essential term of the contract, that consideration received by the defendant-appellant was very inadequate and that performance of the contract would involve hardship on the appellant. 

 5. The learned Subordinate Judge, on consideration of the evidence, oral and documentary, rejected the appellant's pleas and held the agreement (Ext. 2) to be genuine and valid; he found that the appellant received Taka 6 lakh and promised to execute a necessary sale-deed but later on refused to do so and further that the respondent was all along willing and ready to pay the balance of Taka 2 lakh; on these findings, the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court Division thoroughly reassessed the evidence, considered the facts and surrounding circumstances of the case and concurred in the findings of the trial Court and dismissed the appeal. 

 6. The appellant in his leave-petition, challenged all the findings as to execution of the agreement, receipt of the bulk of the consideration and the respondent's readiness to pay the balance of the consideration; but on perusal of the judgments of both the courts below we found no substance in his contention and refused him leave on the findings of facts and thereby closed this chapter. Now we shall go into the question of law to consider which leave was granted. Law on the subject is that the jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, and the Court is no bound to grant it merely because it is lawful to do so. Mr. Khondakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed learned Counsel for the appellant, firstly, contends that respondent-plaintiff is not entitled to relief of specific performance of the contract as he did not deposit the balance of Taka 2 lakh in Court before filing the suit. He contends that making of this deposit is an essential term of the contract which remains to be performed. Referring to section 24 (b) of the Specific Relief Act vis-a-vis the relevant part of the agreement (Ext. 2), he has argued that even if the appellant had not obtained the necessary income-tax and gain-tax clearance certificates it was the respondent's duty to deposit the balance in Court before filing the suit.
